We are so fortunate to have Portsmouth University's Marine Institute,
with its international reputation for providing
high-quality marine research and teaching, on our doorstep, and this
month we welcomed the return of Professor Gordon Watson. He last
presented to us in 2023, and this month, he was able to give updates on
the health of the Solent, our local marine environment.

The Marine Institute's location on the shore of Langstone Harbour is the
perfect location for studying the mesocosm of the Solent; for
investigating the human impact on marine ecosystems and how materials
react to different marine environments.

The Solent has multiple Special Protection Areas; three designated
protection areas are managed and supported by Bird Aware Solent to
safeguard internationally important populations of overwintering and
breeding birds. There are also Marine Conservation Zones and Ramsar
Sites, but increased urbanization, and decreased resilience due to
climate change has caused a decline in habitats.

In order to maintain and increase the protection of this environment,
the Marine Institute knows the importance of highlighting its value in
providing key services such as food, recreation and cultural wellbeing;
services which have been, and which may continue to be overlooked when
planning decisions are made.

Finance is generally the driving force for government policies, and
those involved in the health and conservation of habitats have
increasingly highlighted how natural systems save money. Gordon pointed
out that 1000 tons of nitrogen is naturally sequestered each year by
coastal ecosystems and marine habitats in the Solent, saving around one
billion pounds in nutrient services.

Creative minds are needed to think of new ways forward in research, and
in bringing public awareness to the importance of caring for our natural
resources. The Institute of Marine Sciences has played a foundational
role in launching the Sea Angling Classic; a competition with a prize of
£10,000. Anglers go fishing under controlled conditions, then they
record and release their catch. The data collected, about numbers of
fish, and their location when caught, helps guide further action in
caring for the sea life. Fish generally in focus for the competition
include smooth hound, tope, sea bass, skates, rays and sea bream.

Gordon asked us to guess the most financially valuable fishing activity,
and many were surprised to hear that bait digging, with king ragworm
selling at up to £65 a kilogram was the leader. Dell Quay bait collectors
harvest 5 tons of bait at £160,000 a year. The total amount of bait
collected in the UK each year is about 3000 tons, bringing a return of
around £152,000,000.

Manila clams are gathered by hand in Chichester Harbour and hand
gathering is less damaging than dredging, but new byelaws give daily bag
limits for a number of specified species within designated hand
gathering zones. This is to safeguard the most vulnerable and
ecologically important intertidal areas, so supporting the sustainable
management of the local fisheries and the eco system.

Other fishery catch includes scallops, with, possibly, 47 vessels
dredging for scallops in the winter months.

The Solent offers many services; the salt marsh, mud flats, sea grass
and the renewal of the depleted oyster beds (Portsmouth University are
working with the Blue Marine Foundation to achieve this).

Oyster beds filter the water column, removing nitrogen,
sequestering carbon and providing habitats for hundreds of species.
These habitats bring birds and tourism and the natural systems offer
flood-defence.

Disturbance of the sediment by cockle raking and pump dredging is a
major issue, but satellite images are helping the **I**nshore
**F**isheries and **C**onservation **A**uthorities; the images show
where the dredge lines are, so collecting data to better manage the
Solent fisheries.

The eco system is affected by many pollutants. Two species of marine
worm were collected from sediment and were checked for metal
concentrations. They were found to contain, silver, arsenic, iron, lead,
zinc, cadmium and copper; showing heavy concentrations of metals in the
sediment. The metals may come from industry and possibly industry which
happened in the past, but the hulls of ships are also a probable cause
with their sacrificial anodes of zinc and aluminium; their anti-fouling
paint of copper and zinc and their exhaust scrubbers. An estimated 100
tons of copper and 471 tonnes of all heavy metals seep or discharge into
the Solent each year.

Gordon mentioned possible future hazards to the eco system of the Solent
as there are a number of historic landfill sites close to the shores of
the Solent, such as the one at Fareham Creek. These landfill sites may
be releasing chemicals into the sea especially during increasing
flooding events.

The Environment Agency has collected water quality data from locations
along the coast over the last 25 years, but it isn't consistent or easy
to understand, however, it does look as though the water quality in the
Solent is improving. In Langstone Harbour, data suggests that dissolved
oxygen levels are good and phytoplankton levels high, but the harbour
still faces environmental pressures from untreated sewage and run off
from the land.

Portsmouth University hired nitrate sensors to test the water at
Langstone and in the river Hamble and the sensors showed spikes in
nitrite and nitrate. These spikes impact the health of the sea grass but
some remediation has been achieved by local groups involved with
Portsmouth University**:** this initiative links the recovery of
seagrass meadows with the restoration of adjacent saltmarshes and native
oyster reefs. There are also trials to grow sugar kelp on ropes. The
kelp grows 50-50cms in 4 weeks and it has many uses: it rapidly absorbs
excess nutrients, so starving harmful algae and preventing blooms; it
mitigates acidification; traps particles and sequesters carbon.

Agriculture and shipping are some of the main culprits which pollute our
seas with toxic chemicals and metals, but a lot of first aid is
happening. It now needs to be joined up around the UK.

Nature has the answers and hopefully the research and improvements
already in place will encourage us to work with it, rather than against
it
